title: Vasquez: justifying faith is assent not perfect understanding; against Calvin exact knowledge
source_text: XXX. Similia docet Vasquez in primam secundae, Difput. 209. capite 3. ubi titulus Capitis est, Fidem justificantem non esse perfectam intelligentiam mysteriorum, sed assensum, monstratur. Ex eo enim quod dicit Calvinus lib. 3. Institutionis, cap. 2. Non ignorantia, nec sensus nostri submissio, sed cognitione certa & explorata regnum caelorum adipisci. Colligit Calvinum, & qui eum sequuntur, in fidelibus singulis requirere tanquam ad fidem plane necessariam accuratam & distinctam cognitionem dogmatum fidei, per quam aliquis novit ea recte explicare, defendere, & aliis tradere. Contra quod ibi pertendit fidem non requirere exactam rei creditae intelligentiam & scientiam, sed solum assensum rei creditae propter testimonium. Sicut, inquit, experimento didicimus rudes revera credere multa quae neque aliis tradere, nec defendere sciunt rationibus, sed sola authoritate testimonii muniti eorum assensum habent. Et hoc sat est ad fidem justificantem. Itaque non removet a fide tanquam minus necessariam simpliciter omnem rei creditae notitiam & apprehensionem, sed exploratam tantum, ut loquitur, & exactam notitiam & scientiam, quae multo magis penetrat rem creditam, quam simplex cognitio fidei.
pass_a_gloss: Vasquez teaches similar things in the prima secundae, Disp. 209, chapter 3, whose title is: It is shown that justifying faith is not perfect understanding of the mysteries, but assent. From Calvin saying (Inst. 3.2) that the kingdom of heaven is obtained not by ignorance or by submission of our sense, but by certain and explored cognition, Vasquez gathers that Calvin and his followers require in each of the faithful, as plainly necessary to faith, an accurate and distinct cognition of the dogmas of faith by which someone knows how to explain, defend, and hand them on to others. Against this he maintains that faith does not require exact understanding and science of the thing believed, but only assent to the thing believed on account of testimony. As we have learned by experience, he says, the unlearned truly believe many things which they neither know how to hand on to others nor defend with reasons, but have their assent fortified by the authority of testimony alone; and this is enough for justifying faith. So he does not remove from faith as simply less necessary every notitia and apprehension of the thing believed, but only the explored and exact notitia and science which penetrates the thing believed far more than the simple cognition of faith.
pass_b_english: Vasquez Disp. 209.3: justifying faith is assent, not perfect understanding of the mysteries.

Against a Calvinist-sounding demand for accurate distinct cognition able to explain and defend dogmas, he holds that rude believers assenting on testimony alone have enough for justifying faith; only explored exact science is excluded, not every notitia.
